quote: Alcohol: CIWA-Ar q4h through the risk window; step down only after sustained low scores
problem: Presents q4h as the CIWA-Ar reassessment interval for the whole risk window. Symptom-triggered protocols reassess hourly (or every 1-2 h) while scores are at or above the treatment threshold and move to q4h only once scores stay below it.
whyItMatters: Symptom-triggered dosing is only safe with frequent reassessment. A learner writing or checking orders at q4h for a patient with active, rising withdrawal would under-treat through the window when seizures and DTs develop.
evidence: Saitz et al., JAMA 1994 (symptom-triggered CIWA-Ar trial: hourly assessment while score >=8, spacing out once below threshold); ASAM Clinical Practice Guideline on Alcohol Withdrawal Management 2020 (frequent reassessment during symptom-triggered treatment).
correction: Alcohol: CIWA-Ar q1h while scores are at or above the treatment threshold, then q4h once below it, through the risk window; step down only after sustained low scores

quote: counsel about means honestly, on population-level evidence; Shank et al. 2026
problem: Shank 2026 (Inj Prev) reviews only population-level interventions: firearm laws evaluated with ecological designs. The annotation then frames firearm counselling as resting on that weak population-level evidence. It leaves out the strong individual-level evidence that access to a firearm in the home raises suicide risk.
whyItMatters: A learner may conclude that firearm lethal-means counselling for an individual patient has little evidence behind it, and counsel half-heartedly or skip firearm access at discharge.
evidence: Shank et al., Inj Prev 2026;32(1):7-15 (PMID 40185617): the abstract limits its scope to population-level firearm interventions and says 'The ecological level of analysis precluded individual-level causal inference.' Individual-level evidence: Studdert et al., NEJM 2020;382:2220-9, a cohort study of handgun ownership in California (suicide HR about 3.3 for men and about 7.2 for women); Anglemyer et al., Ann Intern Med 2014 (firearm access OR about 3 for suicide).
correction: counsel about means honestly: the policy-level evidence is weak, but individual-level cohort evidence that household firearm access raises suicide risk is strong (Studdert et al., NEJM 2020); Shank et al. 2026
verified: PubMed metadata/abstract for PMID 40185617 (confirms population-level/ecological scope); Studdert 2020 by recall

quote: For trauma: The Body Keeps the Score is the standard patient/family resource;
problem: The overlay calls a contested popular book 'the standard' trauma resource. Its claims about traumatic memory being stored in the body, and several of the treatments it champions (neurofeedback, yoga, and similar as core PTSD treatment), go beyond or against current evidence. PTSD guidelines put trauma-focused psychotherapy (CPT, PE) first-line, and the book does not.
whyItMatters: A learner will treat and recommend the book as the evidence-based default. Patients and families can then be steered away from first-line trauma-focused therapy or toward unproven treatments.
evidence: VA/DoD PTSD CPG 2023 and American Psychological Association PTSD Clinical Practice Guideline 2017 (trauma-focused psychotherapies CPT/PE/EMDR first-line); published critiques of the book's memory and neuroscience claims (e.g., McNally's work on traumatic memory).
correction: For trauma: The Body Keeps the Score is widely read but its neuroscience and treatment claims are contested — pair it with the message that trauma-focused therapy (CPT/PE) is first-line;

quote: Gabor Maté's trauma-informed understanding of ADHD—links attention challenges to stress and development.
problem: The annotation presents, without qualification, Maté's thesis that ADHD comes mainly from early stress and attachment disruption. That view departs from the consensus that ADHD is a neurodevelopmental disorder with high heritability.
whyItMatters: A learner may believe, or tell families, that ADHD is caused by early stress or parenting. That misstates the etiology and can blame parents, in a curated section that learners use to recommend books to families.
evidence: Faraone & Larsson, Mol Psychiatry 2019 (mean twin heritability about 74%); World Federation of ADHD International Consensus Statement, Faraone et al., Neurosci Biobehav Rev 2021.
correction: Gabor Maté's trauma-informed understanding of ADHD—links attention challenges to stress and development; note that this environmental view departs from the evidence that ADHD is highly heritable (twin heritability about 74%).

quote: rewires subconscious beliefs so you no longer want to drink.
problem: The page states the publisher's efficacy claim as fact. The book has no controlled-trial evidence, and the Addiction section does not mention that alcohol use disorder has effective treatments.
whyItMatters: A learner recommending it to a patient with AUD may present it as effective, standing in for evidence-based treatment (naltrexone or acamprosate, psychosocial care) rather than a supplementary read.
evidence: No RCT evidence for the book's method; APA Practice Guideline for Pharmacological Treatment of AUD 2018 (naltrexone and acamprosate recommended).
correction: aims to change beliefs about alcohol so drinking loses its appeal (a popular self-help read, not an evidence-based treatment; pair with AUD medication and therapy options).

problem: The title is cut to 'I Hate You'. The book is 'I Hate You—Don't Leave Me: Understanding the Borderline Personality' (revised edition 2021). There is also no annotation.
whyItMatters: A learner recommending the book to a family by the title shown would name it wrongly and could cause offence. The full title carries the book's meaning.
evidence: Kreisman JJ, Straus H. I Hate You—Don't Leave Me: Understanding the Borderline Personality, revised and updated edition, TarcherPerigee 2021 (ISBN 9780593418499).
correction: **[I Hate You—Don't Leave Me](https://www.amazon.com/dp/0593418492)** — Jerold Kreisman & Hal Straus.
verified: recall (ISBN on page matches the 2021 revised edition)
